paragraphs.text: OF WHAT THINGS THE RITES PERFORMED IN THE HOLY CHURCH AT THE SYNAXIS ARE SYMBOLS. PROLOGUE. How the wise man becomes wiser when he is given an occasion, and how the righteous man, once he has come to know, will add to his learning, as the divine Proverb says: you yourself, most honored of all to me, have shown this clearly by experience. You have taught by deed what the divine word wisely hints at. Not long ago you heard me relating briefly and in passing, as far as I could, what another man had said: a certain great elder, truly wise in divine things. He had contemplated, nobly and mystically, the holy Church and the holy synaxis celebrated in it, and had expounded these things as a teacher would. You at once asked me [?] Maximus the monk, on ecclesiastical mystagogy [?]

to make a written account of these things for you. You wanted to have the writing as a remedy for forgetfulness and an aid to memory. Memory, you said, naturally has time as its conqueror, and time can imperceptibly, through forgetfulness, rob it of the impressions and images of the good things stored in it and wipe them out altogether. For this reason memory certainly needs some means of renewal, by which the power of the word, always in full vigor, naturally keeps memory unharmed and undiminished. How much wiser it is to seek a lasting permanence for what one has heard, rather than merely to hear it, anyone knows who cares even a little for the nobility of reason and is not wholly a stranger to kinship with the word.

At first I hesitated and declined the subject (for the truth shall be told). It was not that I did not wish to give you, beloved, what you desired by every means and as far as I could. It was that I had no share in the grace that leads the worthy to such a task. Nor had I experience of the power and practice of speaking, since I was brought up in plainness and am entirely uninitiated in the arts of rhetoric, whose charm lies only in delivery. Most people delight in these above all, confining their pleasure to the ear, even when such words often contain nothing of value in their depths. And, to put it more properly and truly, I was afraid that the poverty of my words would insult that blessed man's lofty speech and understanding of divine things. Nevertheless, I later yielded to the force of love, which is stronger than all things, and willingly accepted the command. I chose rather to be laughed at by fault-finders for presumption and ignorance, for the sake of obedience, than to be thought by you, through delay, unwilling to share your eagerness for every good thing. I cast the care of how to speak upon God, who alone works wonders. He teaches man knowledge and makes plain the tongue of the stammerer. He devises a way for those who have none. He raises the poor man from the earth and lifts the needy from the dunghill: I mean from the mind of the flesh and the foul-smelling mire of the passions. By the poor man I mean the one poor in spirit, or the one who is poor in wickedness and lacks its habit. Or, on the contrary, I mean the one still held by the law of the flesh and by the passions, and for that reason poor and lacking in the grace of virtue and knowledge.

Now the all-holy and truly God-revealing Dionysius the Areopagite, in his treatise On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, has contemplated the symbols of the sacred rite [?]

of the holy synaxis in a manner worthy of his greatness of mind. Therefore it must be understood that the present discourse does not go over the same things, nor does it proceed along the same paths as he did. It would be rash, presumptuous and close to madness for one who can neither contain nor understand his works to try to take them in hand, and to put forward as his own the mysteries revealed by inspiration through the Spirit to him alone. This discourse deals only with what he, by the will of God, lovingly left to others as within their grasp. He left these things for them to expound, and for the exercise of their own disposition toward divine things according to their desire. Through them the all-radiant ray of the rites, contemplated in proportion to each person, becomes known, and holds to itself those whom longing has seized. So those who come after him need not be entirely idle throughout the whole day of the time [?] of this present life, lacking the word that hires them for that divine work in the vineyard. That word, in return for spiritual labor in the spiritual vineyard, pays the spiritual denarius of the divine and most royal image, which the evil one plundered by deceit in the beginning, when the commandment was transgressed.

I do not promise to relate in order everything that the blessed elder contemplated mystically. Nor do I promise to relate even what I do say as he understood it and said it. For he was a philosopher and a teacher of all learning. Beyond that, through his abundance of virtue and his long and most skilled practice and labor in divine things, he had made himself free from the bonds of matter and from the fantasies that go with it. So, naturally, his mind was illumined by divine rays, and he could see at once what the many do not see. His speech was a most precise interpreter of what he understood. Like a mirror unhindered by any stain of passion, it could purely carry and express things that others cannot even understand. His hearers could see his whole mind riding upon his words, and everything he had understood shining purely in his whole mind, and they could receive it as it passed to them through the medium of speech. But I will relate only what I carry in memory, what I can understand dimly and express still more dimly, [?] piously, by the grace of God who illumines what is darkened. You know how to judge justly, and I do not suppose that you think I can understand or speak otherwise than as I am able, and as grace from above grants. It provides fittingly the power proportioned to me, even if the one who handed these things down and taught them is most sublime. To seek equal results from those who are not equal in virtue and knowledge seems to me not far from trying to show that the moon gives light equally with the sun [?]

and trying to force things that do not wholly agree with one another to agree in every respect. That cannot be done; it is impossible. [?] as the cause of being, it denies all beings of itself. And again, properly speaking, no name fits it, since none presents what the thing sought is in its very essence and nature. For nothing at all is naturally joined to it as its cause, whether being or non-being. So nothing that exists and is spoken of, and nothing that does not exist and is not spoken of, can reasonably be said to come near it. Its existence is simple, unknowable and inaccessible to all. It is entirely beyond interpretation, and beyond every affirmation and negation. So much for these matters. Let us come to the proposed subject of the discourse.

CHAPTER 1. How and in what manner the holy Church is an image and figure of God.

That blessed elder used to say that the holy Church, at the first level of contemplation, bears the figure and image of God, since by imitation and figure it has the same activity as he has. God made all things by his infinite power and brought them into being. He holds them together, gathers them and sets their bounds. In his providence he binds them to one another and to himself, both intelligible things and sensible things. Around himself, as cause, beginning and end, he holds all things together. Things that by nature stand apart from one another he makes converge with one another, by the single power of their relation to him as their beginning. By this power

all things are led to an identity of movement and existence in which nothing is destroyed and nothing is confused. No being is primarily at odds with or divided from any other by a difference of nature or of movement. All have grown together with all, without confusion, through the single, indissoluble relation to the one sole beginning and cause, and its protection. This relation cancels and veils all the particular relations seen in each being according to its nature. It does not do so by destroying them, abolishing them or making them cease to exist. It does so by overcoming them and appearing above them, as the whole appears above its parts, or rather as the cause of the whole itself appears. Through that cause both the whole itself and the parts of the whole naturally appear and exist, since their cause shines wholly above them. And as the sun, shining out, veils the nature and power of the stars, so the cause veils the existence of its effects. For just as parts naturally come from the whole, so effects naturally come from the cause. They properly exist and are known, and their own property comes to rest [?], when they are caught up in their reference to the cause and qualified by it throughout, according to the single power of their relation to it, as has been said. For God, who is all in all, being beyond all in infinite measure, will be seen alone by those who are pure in mind. This will happen when the mind, gathering up in contemplation the principles (logoi) of beings, comes to rest in God himself. He is the cause, beginning and end of the production and coming into being of all things, and the ground, without extension, that encompasses them all.

In the same way the holy Church of God will be shown to work the same things in our regard as God does, being an image of its archetype. Many people come into it and are reborn and re-created by it in the Spirit: men, women and children, almost infinite in number. They are divided from one another and differ greatly in race and kind, in nations and languages, in ways of life and ages, in opinions and crafts, in manners, customs and pursuits, and again in knowledge and rank, in fortunes, characters and habits. Yet the Church gives and grants to all equally one divine form and name: to be of Christ and to be called after Christ. It also gives one relation according to faith, simple, without parts and undivided. This relation does not allow the many countless differences in each person to be noticed, even though they exist [?], because all are referred and gathered universally into the Church. In it no one is in any way separated from the common whole. All have grown together with one another and

are joined by the one grace and power of faith, simple and undivided. For "the multitude of them all," it says, "were of one heart and one soul." So from different members there is, and is seen to be, one body, truly worthy of Christ himself, our true head. In him, says the divine Apostle, "there is neither male nor female, neither Jew nor Greek, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither slave nor free, but he himself is all and in all." He encloses all things in himself by the one simple and infinitely wise power of his goodness. He is like a center from which straight lines extend, by one simple and unified cause and power. He does not let the beginnings of beings break away along with their extremities, but bounds their extensions in a circle and draws to himself the distinct beings that came into existence through him. He does this so that the creatures and works of the one God may not be wholly alien and hostile to one another, with nothing around which, and no place where, they could show friendship, peace and identity toward one another. He also does it so that their very being may not risk falling into non-being by being separated from God.

The holy Church, then, as has been said, is an image of God. Among the faithful it works the same union that God works, even if those made one in it through faith differ in their characteristics and come from different places and ways of life. God himself naturally works this union among the essences of beings without confusion. As has been shown, he softens their difference and makes them one by their reference to and union with himself as their cause, beginning and end.

CHAPTER 2. How and in what manner the holy Church of God is an image of the world, which consists of visible and invisible essences.

At a second level of contemplation, he said that the holy Church of God is a figure and image of the whole world, which consists of visible and invisible essences, since the Church admits the same union and distinction as the world. The Church is one house in its construction, but it admits a difference through the particular arrangement of its form. It is divided into the place reserved for priests and ministers alone, which we call the sanctuary, and the place open for all the faithful people to enter, which we call the nave. Again, it is one in its substance. It is not divided along with its parts because of the difference between those parts. Rather, by referring the parts themselves to its own unity, it frees them from the difference in their names, and [?]

shows that both are the same as each other. It declares that each is to the other, by interchange, what each is to itself. The nave is a sanctuary in potency, being consecrated by its reference to the goal of the mystagogy. Conversely, the sanctuary is a nave, since it holds the beginning of its own mystagogy in actuality. Through both, the Church remains one and the same.

So too with the whole world of beings that God brought into existence by creation. It is divided into the intelligible world, filled with intellectual and bodiless essences, and this sensible, bodily world, magnificently woven together from many forms and natures. It is like another Church, not made with hands, which this Church made with hands wisely reveals. It has the world above as its sanctuary, so to speak, assigned to the powers above, and the world below as its nave, allotted to those whose lot is to live through the senses. Again, the world is one and is not divided along with its parts. On the contrary, it bounds even the difference between the parts that comes from their natural properties, by referring them to its own unity and indivisibility. It shows that they are the same as itself and as one another, without confusion and by interchange, and that each has entered wholly into the whole of the other. Both, as parts, fill it up as one whole, and both, as parts, are filled up by it as a whole, in a unified and complete way. For the whole intelligible world appears, to those who are able to see, mystically imprinted on the whole sensible world in symbolic forms. And the whole sensible world exists within the whole intelligible world, simplified into its principles by the mind's knowledge. The sensible world is in the intelligible by its principles, and the intelligible is in the sensible by its figures, and their work is one, "as it were a wheel within a wheel," says Ezekiel, the marvelous seer of great things. He is speaking, I think, of the two worlds. And again the divine Apostle says: "For his invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that are made." If what does not appear is seen through what appears, as it is written, then much more will what appears be understood through what does not appear, by those devoted to spiritual contemplation. For the symbolic contemplation of intelligible things through visible things is the same as the spiritual knowledge and understanding of visible things through invisible ones. Things that point to each other must surely reflect each other truly and clearly, and keep their relation to each other unbroken.

CHAPTER 3. That the holy Church of God is also an image of the sensible world alone.

And again he said that the holy Church of God is a symbol of the sensible world alone, taken by itself. Its divine sanctuary is heaven, and the beauty of its nave is earth. In the same way the world is a Church: heaven is like its sanctuary, and the adornment of the earth is like its nave.

CHAPTER 4. How and in what manner the holy Church of God symbolically images man, and is itself imaged by him as a man.

And again, by another mode of contemplation, he said that the holy Church of God is a man. The sanctuary is its soul, the divine altar its mind, and the nave its body. So it is an image and likeness of man, who was made according to the image and likeness of God. Through the nave, as through a body, it puts forward moral philosophy. Through the sanctuary, as through a soul, it spiritually expounds natural contemplation. Through the divine altar, as through a mind, it reveals mystical theology. And conversely, he said that man is a mystical Church. Through the body, as through a nave, he makes the active part of the soul shine with virtue by carrying out the commandments, according to moral philosophy. Through the soul, as through a sanctuary, he offers to God through reason, according to natural contemplation, the principles of the senses, purely circumcised from matter in the Spirit. Through the mind, as through an altar, he calls upon the silence, much-hymned in the innermost places, of the invisible and unknown great voice of the Godhead, and he calls upon it through another silence, eloquent and many-voiced. As far as a man can, he enters into communion with it according to mystical theology. He becomes what one must be who has been found worthy of God's indwelling and has been marked with God's all-radiant splendors.

CHAPTER 5. How and in what manner the holy Church of God is an image and figure of the soul considered by itself.

He taught that the holy Church can be an image not only of the whole man, made up of soul and body joined together, but also of the soul itself, considered by itself in thought. For he said that the soul as a whole consists of an intellectual power and a vital power. The intellectual power moves freely by its will. The vital power remains by nature as it is, without choice. Again, he said that the intellectual power contains the contemplative part and the active part. The contemplative part, he said, is called mind, and the active part reason. Of the intellectual power

the mind is the mover, and of the vital power reason is the provident guardian. The one, I mean the mind, is and is called wisdom when it keeps its movements toward God wholly unchanging. Likewise reason is and is called prudence when it soberly joins to the mind, through its activities, the vital power that it governs providentially, and shows that power to be no different from the mind, bearing through virtue the same and a similar reflection of the divine. This vital power, he said, is naturally shared between mind and reason. So the soul is, and is shown to consist primarily of, mind and reason, being intellectual and rational, while the vital power is seen equally in both, I mean in mind and in reason. For it is not right to think that either of them lacks a share in life, since life is distributed between them both [?]. Through this, the mind, which we said is called wisdom, unfolds by its contemplative habit in ineffable silence and knowledge, and is led to the truth through unforgetting and unceasing knowledge. Reason, which we called prudence, by its active habit comes bodily, according to virtue, through faith, to its end in the good. From both of these is formed the true knowledge of divine and human things, the truly unerring knowledge, which is the goal of the whole, most divine philosophy of the Christians.

To speak more clearly about these matters: he said that one part of the soul is contemplative, as has been said, and the other active. He called the contemplative part mind and the active part reason, these being the first powers of the soul. Again, he called mind wisdom and reason prudence, these being its first activities. And setting it out in detail, he said that the soul has, in its intellectual part, mind, wisdom, contemplation, knowledge and unforgetting knowledge, and the end of these is truth. In its rational part it has reason, prudence, action, virtue and faith, and the end of these is the good. He said that truth and the good signify God. Truth signifies him when the divine seems to be indicated from its essence. For truth is simple, single, one, identical, without parts, unchangeable, impassible, unerring and wholly without extension. The good signifies him when the divine is indicated from its activity. For the good does good, provides for all that comes from it and protects it. According to the opinion of the etymologists, the word comes from "being exceedingly" (agan einai), or from "having been placed," or from "placing" [?], since it grants to all beings their being, their continuance and their movement. [?] is "being exceedingly," or "having been placed," or "running"; we would say [?]

He said, then, that the five pairs understood in the soul revolve around the one pair that signifies God. By "pair" I mean here intellect and reason; wisdom and prudence; contemplation and action; knowledge and virtue; unforgetting knowledge and faith. The pair that signifies the divine is truth and the good. Moved by these step by step, the soul is united to the God of all things. It imitates the immutability and the beneficence of his essence and activity through a habit of the good that is firm and unchangeable in its free choice. And to mix in a small contemplation that fits these things: perhaps this is the divine decad of strings on the spiritual psaltery of the soul. With the word sounding in harmony with the Spirit, through the other blessed decad of the commandments, it produces in the mind notes that are perfect, harmonious and melodious, by which God is hymned. So I may learn the meaning of the decad that [?] plays and of the decad that is sung. And when decad is mystically united and joined with decad, it brings back to himself Jesus, my God and Saviour, who is made complete through me as I am saved, though he is always entirely full and can never depart from himself. And it wondrously restores me, the human being, to myself, or rather to God, from whom I have received my being and toward whom I hasten, longing from afar to receive well-being as well. Whoever has come to know this by experiencing what is spoken of will certainly know it, having already recognized his own dignity clearly through experience. He will know how what is "according to the image" is restored to the image; how the archetype is honoured; what the power of the mystery of our salvation is, and for whose sake Christ died; how, again, we can abide in him and he in us, as he said; and how "the word of the Lord is upright, and all his works are done in faithfulness." But let us bring the discussion back to its proper sequence, and content ourselves with what has been said on these matters. He said that the intellect, moved through wisdom, comes to contemplation; through contemplation, to knowledge; through knowledge, to unforgetting knowledge; and through unforgetting knowledge, to truth. At truth the intellect receives the limit of its movement, being circumscribed (Ps. 32:4).

[?] ... the unceasing and settled perpetual movement concerning what is knowable beyond all knowledge, whose limit, as the knowable that cannot be forgotten, is the truth. This too is worthy of wonder: how the incomprehensible comes to an end by being circumscribed, namely by being bounded by God, the truth. For God is the truth. The intellect moves around him unceasingly and without forgetting, and can never cease from its movement, because it finds no limit where there is no interval. For the wondrous greatness of the divine infinity is something [?] without parts and wholly without extension, and it admits no comprehension of any kind that could reach it so as to know what it is in its essence. And what has no extension, and can in no way be comprehended, is bounded by nothing. In the same way, he said, reason, moved through prudence, comes to action; through action, to virtue; and through virtue, to faith, which is the truly firm and unfailing assurance of divine things. Reason first has faith potentially through prudence, and later displays it actually through virtue, as it is made manifest in works. For "faith without works is dead," as it is written, and no one of sound mind would ever dare to count anything dead and inactive among good things. Through faith reason comes to the good, where it reaches its end and ceases from its own activities, its potency, habit and activity being circumscribed. For he said that prudence is the potency of reason, and that reason is potentially prudence; action is its habit, and virtue its activity. Faith is the inward and unalterable fixity of prudence, action and virtue, that is, of potency, habit and activity. Its ultimate limit is the good, and there reason comes to the end of its movement and ceases. For God is the good, in whom every power of every reason naturally [?] finds its limit. How and in what way each of these is achieved and brought into act, what is opposed or akin to each of them, and to what degree, are questions the present subject does not allow us to distinguish and discuss. It is enough to know this much. Every soul may, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and its own diligence and zeal, become able to join and weave these together: reason with intellect, prudence with wisdom, action with contemplation, virtue with knowledge, and faith with unforgetting knowledge, so that none falls short of the other or exceeds it, and all excess and deficiency are cut away. To put it briefly, it may become able to make its own decad a monad. Then it too will be united to God,

who is true and good, one and only. It becomes beautiful and magnificent, and as far as possible like him, through the completion of the four generic virtues. These indicate the divine decad in the soul and contain the other blessed decad of the commandments. For the tetrad is potentially a decad, since it is composed from the monad by successive progression. And again, the same tetrad is a monad, because by convergence it contains the good in a unitary way and shows the simple, indivisible character of the divine activity, divided among [?] without being divided. Through these virtues the soul has vigorously kept what is its own unassailable, and has manfully beaten off what is alien as evil. Its intellect is rational, its wisdom prudent, its contemplation active, its knowledge virtuous, and on top of these it has unforgetting knowledge, most faithful and unchangeable. It has offered to God effects soberly joined to their causes and activities to their powers, and in exchange for them it receives the deification that produces simplicity. For reason is the activity and manifestation of intellect, as an effect is of its cause; so too prudence is that of wisdom, action of contemplation, virtue of knowledge, and faith of unforgetting knowledge. From these is fashioned the inward relation to truth and the good, that is, to God. He said this relation is divine science, unerring knowledge, love and peace, in which and through which deification comes. It is science, as the completion of all the knowledge of God and divine things that human beings can attain, and the unerring sum of the virtues. It is knowledge, as having genuinely reached the truth and as granting a lasting experience of the divine. It is love, as sharing wholly by disposition in the whole delight of God. It is peace, as undergoing the same things as God and preparing those found worthy of it to undergo them too. For the divine is entirely unmoved, since nothing at all can disturb it (what could even reach its height?). And peace is an unshakable and unmoved steadiness, and moreover an undisturbed joy. If so, does not every soul found worthy to receive divine peace undergo divine things? It has passed beyond vice and ignorance, falsehood and wickedness, the evils opposed to virtue and knowledge, to truth and the good, which have a parasitic existence alongside the soul's movements contrary to nature. Beyond these, if it is lawful to say so, it has already passed even the bounds of virtue itself and of knowledge, and of truth and goodness as we know them. Ineffably and unknowably it has laid itself to rest in the more-than-true and more-than-good bed of God, according to his most truthful promise. So nothing that naturally disturbs it can any longer reach its hiddenness in God. In that blessed and all-

holy bed the awesome mystery of a union beyond intellect and reason is accomplished. Through it God and the soul will become one flesh and one spirit: God with the Church, that is, the soul, and the soul with God. O Christ, how I wonder at your goodness! I will not dare to say "how I hymn it," for I do not have power enough even to wonder at it worthily. "For the two shall become one flesh. This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church," says the divine Apostle. And again: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." So when the soul has become unified, gathered both to itself and to God, there will no longer be any reasoning that divides it into many in thought. Its head has been crowned by the first, only and one Word and God. In him, in one incomprehensible simplicity, all the principles of beings both are and subsist in unity, since he is the creator and maker of beings. The soul gazes on him, not as outside itself but as wholly present in it as a whole, and by a simple apprehension it too will know the principles and causes of beings. Before it was wedded to the Word and God, it was perhaps led through these principles by the methods of division, and was carried by them savingly and harmoniously to him who contains and makes every principle and every cause. These things belong to the soul, then, as we have said. In the intellect it has wisdom potentially, from wisdom contemplation, from contemplation knowledge, and from knowledge unforgetting knowledge, through which it is led to truth as the limit and end of the goods of the intellect. In reason it has prudence, from prudence action, from action virtue, and from virtue faith, by which it reaches the good as the blessed end of rational activities. Through all these, by the convergence of their union with one another, the science of divine things is gathered. To all these the holy Church of God clearly corresponds [?], for in contemplation it is likened to the soul. Through the sanctuary it signifies all that belongs to the intellect and has been shown to proceed from the intellect. Through the nave it makes clear all that belongs to reason and has been shown to come from reason by distinction. And it gathers all things toward the mystery celebrated on the divine altar. Whoever has been able to be initiated into this mystery prudently and wisely, through what is celebrated in the Church, has made his own soul truly a Church of God, and divine. Perhaps it was for the sake of this soul, and as a model of it, that the Church made by hands, which through the variety of divine things within it is wisely
a model by way of symbol, was handed down to us as guidance toward what is better.

How and in what way holy Scripture too is called a man. In the contemplation of the higher sense he said that the Church is a spiritual man and that man is a mystical Church. In the same way he said that the whole of holy Scripture, taken together, is a man. The Old Testament is its body, and the New is its soul, spirit and intellect. And again, of the whole of holy Scripture, Old and New, the historical letter is the body, while the sense of what is written, and the goal to which that sense is directed, is the soul. When I heard this I particularly admired the precision of the comparison, and as far as I could I duly praised him who distributes gifts to each according to his worth. For a man like us is mortal in what is seen but immortal in what is not seen. In the same way holy Scripture has a visible letter that passes away, while the spirit hidden in the letter never ceases to exist, and this confirms the truth of the contemplation. And just as a man like us withers the flesh when through philosophy he masters passionate desire and impulse, so holy Scripture, when understood spiritually, circumcises its own letter. For the divine Apostle says, "As much as our outer man is wasting away, so much is the inner man renewed day by day." Let this be understood and said of holy Scripture too, understood figuratively as a man. For as much as its letter recedes, so much does its spirit gain ground. And as much as the shadows of temporary worship pass away, so much does the truth of faith come in, all-radiant, wholly shining and without shadow. It is above all according to this truth and for its sake that Scripture both exists and was written. And it is called Scripture because it is inscribed on the intellect by spiritual grace. So too a man like us, because of the rational and intellectual soul, above all both is and is called a man. According to this soul and through it he is the image and likeness of God who made him, and he is set apart by nature from the other living creatures, having no trace whatever of [?] power in common with them. How the world is called a man, and in what way man is called a world. Following this image again, in a fitting imitation, the whole world, which consists

of visible and invisible things, he proposed to be a man, and conversely man, made up of soul and body, to be a world. For he said that intelligible things hold the place of soul, as the soul is among intelligible things, and that sensible things hold the figure of body, as the body is among sensible things. Intelligible things are the soul of sensible things, and sensible things the body of intelligible things. The intelligible world is in the sensible world as a soul is in a body, and the sensible world is joined to the intelligible as a body is to a soul. And there is one world made up of both, just as there is one man made up of soul and body. Neither of these, naturally grown together in union, denies or casts off the other, because of the law of him who bound them together. In this law the principle of the unifying power has been sown. It does not allow their identity by hypostasis in the union to be ignored because of their difference in nature. Nor does it allow the property that circumscribes each of them in itself to prove stronger, so as to separate and divide them, than the bond of kinship mystically placed in them by the union. Through this kinship the one universal mode of the hidden and unknown presence of the cause that holds beings together is present in all things in various ways. It makes all things subsist both in themselves and in one another, unconfused and undivided, and shows them to belong to one another, through their unifying relation, more than to themselves. So it will be until it pleases him who bound them together to loose them, for the sake of a greater and more mystical dispensation, at the time of the universal consummation for which we hope. Then the world too, like a man, will die as to its visible things, and will rise again new from old, in the resurrection expected at any moment. At that time the man like us will also rise together with the world, as a part with the whole and the small with the great, and will receive the power never again to be subject to corruption. Then the body will become like the soul, and sensible things like intelligible things, in beauty and glory. One divine power will appear in all things through a manifest and active presence, in proportion to each, and through itself will keep the bond of union unbroken for endless ages. If anyone wishes, then, to have a life and a word that are dear and pleasing to God, let him greatly value the better and more honourable parts of these three men: the world, holy Scripture, and the man like us. Let him care as much as he can for the soul, which is immortal and divine and will be made god through the virtues. And let him despise the flesh, which is subject to corruption and death, and which, if the soul is neglected, can soil

its dignity. For "a corruptible body," it says, "weighs down the soul, and the earthly tent burdens the mind full of cares." And again: "The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh." And again: "He who sows to his own flesh will reap corruption from the flesh." Let him set his intellect, through understanding, to compete with the bodiless and intellectual powers, leaving behind what is present and seen [?]. "For the things that are seen are temporary," it says, "but the things that are not seen are eternal." In these powers God rests, because of the fullness of their peaceful state. And through wise study of holy Scripture he will rise soberly beyond the letter to the Holy Spirit. He will find him written on the tablets of his heart through the grace that is in the Spirit, as with unveiled face he beholds the glory of God as in a mirror, the veil of the letter having been taken away.

Of what the first entrance of the holy synaxis is a symbol, and of what the rites performed after it are symbols. After this brief account of the contemplations of the holy Church given by the blessed elder, our discussion now comes to give, as far as possible, an even briefer account of the holy synaxis of the Church. He taught that the first entrance of the high priest into the holy church at the sacred synaxis bears the figure and image of the first coming into this world, in the flesh, of the Son of God and our Saviour Christ. By this coming he freed and redeemed human nature, which had been enslaved to corruption, had by its own doing [?] suffered death through sin, and was tyrannically ruled by the devil. He who was without liability and without sin paid the whole debt on its behalf as though he were liable, and led it back again to the original grace of the kingdom. He gave himself for us as a ransom and an exchange, and in return for our corrupting passions he gave his own life-giving passion, a healing remedy and the salvation of the whole world. After this coming, his ascension into heaven and to the throne above the heavens, and his restoration there, are symbolically represented by the high priest's entrance into the sanctuary and his ascent to the priestly throne. Chapter 9. What the entrance of the people into the holy Church of God signifies. The entrance of the people into the church together with the hierarch, the blessed elder said, signifies the turning of unbelievers from ignorance and error [note 37: "held fast," A and Fr.]

to the knowledge of God, and the passage of believers from vice and ignorance to virtue and knowledge. For the entrance into the church does not only point to the turning of unbelievers to the true God. It also points to the correction, through repentance, of each of us who believe but set aside the commandments of the Lord by leading a dissolute and shameful life. Anyone at all, whether a murderer, an adulterer, a thief, arrogant, a boaster, insolent, greedy, avaricious, a slanderer, one who bears grudges, one easily led to rage and anger, a reviler, a false accuser, a whisperer, one easily overcome by envy, or a drunkard (in short, not to lengthen the discussion by listing every kind of vice), whoever is held by any vice whatever, if he stops being willingly held by it as a practice and acting on it deliberately, and changes his life for the better, choosing virtue instead of vice, let such a one be understood and said, properly and truly, to enter together with Christ, God and high priest, into virtue, which is figuratively understood as the Church.

Of what the divine readings are a symbol. The teacher said that the divine readings from the all-holy books suggest the divine and blessed wishes and counsels of the all-holy God. Through them each of us, in proportion to the power within him, receives instructions about what must be done. We also learn the laws of the divine and blessed contests, and by competing lawfully according to them we are counted worthy of the victor's crowns of the kingdom of Christ.

Of what the divine chants are a symbol. He said that the spiritual delight of the divine chants signifies the vivid pleasure of divine goods. This pleasure stirs souls to the pure and blessed love of God, and rouses them even more to hatred of sin. Chapter 12. What the proclamations of peace signify. The wise man distinguished what is meant by the proclamations of peace made from within the sanctuary, at the high priest's command, after each reading. They show the divine approvals brought by the holy angels. By these approvals God decides the contests of those who compete lawfully for the truth against the opposing powers, and the unseen struggles. [Marginal note:] "Wish" is an imaginative desire for things that are in our power and things that are not in our power; or what natural [?]. Fr.: "Counsel," that is, deliberation, is an inquiring desire concerning something to be done among the things in our power. But in God's case [?] are beyond all these: will and counsel and whatever else is predicated of God. [Note 33:] "Of what things they are symbols," A. "Of what it is," Fr.

…dissolving [?], and giving peace by abolishing the body of sin, and granting the saints the grace of dispassion in return for their labours on behalf of virtue; so that, released from warfare, they may turn the powers of the soul to spiritual husbandry, that is, to the working of the virtues. Through these powers they scattered the hordes of the evil spirits, with God the Word as their general, who also broke up the devil's bitter devices, so hard to escape.

What the reading of the holy Gospel, and the mystical rites that follow it, symbolize specifically in the case of each individual. Hence, immediately after these, the sacred ordinance of the holy Church has laid down that the divine reading of the holy Gospel should take place. Specifically, it introduces the hardship that the earnest endure for the sake of the Word. After this the Word, coming to them from heaven as the high priest, so to speak, of gnostic contemplation, draws in the mind of the flesh in them as if it were a kind of sensible world, and drives away the thoughts that still incline toward the earth. From there, through the closing of the doors and the entrance of the holy mysteries, he leads them to the vision of intelligible things, now that they have shut their senses to words and things alike and have come to be outside flesh and world, and he teaches them the ineffable things [?]. They have already been gathered by the kiss to one another and to him, and in return for his great kindness toward them they gratefully offer him only the confession of thanksgiving for their own salvation, which the divine Symbol of faith signifies. Then, having made them numbered with the angels through the Thrice-Holy, and having granted them the same knowledge of sanctifying theology that the angels have, he brings them to God the Father, adopted as sons in the Spirit through the prayer by which they were deemed worthy to call God Father. And from there again, as if they had now knowingly passed through all the principles in beings, he leads them, through the “One is holy” and what follows, unknowably to the unknown Monad, united to it by grace and made like it by participation, in an identity undivided as far as is possible.

What the divine reading of the holy Gospel [?] is a symbol of, and what it signifies in general. … In general, it signifies the consummation of this world. For after the divine reading of the holy Gospel the high priest comes down from the throne, and of the catechumens, and of the rest
[?] … up to “but”; the other things said in between are contemplations following the Gospel. [?] “specifically” [?] refers to [?] “generally” [?]

of those unworthy of the divine contemplation of the mysteries about to be shown, a dismissal and expulsion takes place through the ministers. In itself it signifies and prefigures the truth of which it is the image and type, and it cries out, as it were, through these things that after the gospel of the kingdom has been preached in the whole world, as it is written, as a testimony to all the nations, then the end will come. Then our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ will come at his second coming, from heaven that is, with great glory: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God,” says the divine Apostle. He will take vengeance on his adversaries, and through the holy angels he will separate the faithful from the faithless, the unrighteous from the righteous, and the accursed from the saints; in short, to sum it up, those who walked after the flesh from those who walked by the Spirit of God. And for infinite and endless ages, as the truth of the divine oracles says, he will render to each the just reward his life has deserved. CHAPTER 15. What the closing of the doors of the holy church after the holy Gospel is a symbol of.

The closing of the doors of God's holy church, which takes place after the sacred reading of the holy Gospel and the expulsion of the catechumens, signifies the passing away of material things. It also signifies the entrance of the worthy into the intelligible world, that is, into the bridal chamber of Christ, which will take place after that fearful separation and still more fearful verdict. And it signifies the complete casting off, in the senses, of activity that deception had set to work.

What the entrance of the holy mysteries signifies. The entrance of the holy and august mysteries is, as that great old man said, the beginning and prelude of the new teaching that will be given in heaven about God's dispensation toward us. It is also the revelation of the mystery of our salvation, which lies in the innermost sanctuary of the divine hiddenness. “For I will not drink from now on of the fruit of the vine,” says God the Word to his disciples, “until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.”
What the divine kiss is a symbol of. The spiritual kiss proclaimed to all foreshadows the concord that all will have with one another at the time

of the revelation of the ineffable good things to come, in faith and love, in concord and like-mindedness and rational identity, through which the worthy receive their kinship with God the Word. For the mouth is a symbol of the Word (logos). Through the Word above all, all who share in reason, as rational beings, are joined with one another and with the first and only [?] Word, the cause of all reason.

What the divine Symbol of faith signifies. The confession of the divine Symbol of faith made by all foreshadows the mystical thanksgiving that will be offered in the age to come for the marvellous principles and modes of God's all-wise providence toward us, by which we were saved. Through it the worthy show themselves grateful for the divine kindness, since apart from this they have nothing else at all to offer in return for the infinite divine goods bestowed on them.

What the doxology of the Thrice-Holy signifies. The threefold cry of sanctification in the divine hymnody, raised by all the faithful people, signifies the union and equality of honour with the bodiless and intellectual powers that will appear in the future. In that state human nature will be taught to hymn and sanctify the one Godhead in three hypostases with a threefold sanctification, in harmony with the powers above, because it will share their unchanging and everlasting motion around God. What the holy prayer “Our Father who art in heaven” is a symbol of. The all-holy and venerable invocation of the great and blessed God and Father is a symbol of the adoption that will be given, real and subsistent, by the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit. In that adoption every human particularity will be overcome and veiled by the coming of grace, and all the saints will be called sons of God and will be such: all who even now, through the virtues, have brightened themselves splendidly and gloriously with the divine beauty of goodness.

What the end of the mystical rite signifies, with what is proclaimed there, that is, “One is Holy, one is Lord,” and what follows. The confession of “One is Holy” and what follows, made by all the people at the end of the mystical rite, [signifies] the gathering and union of those who have been perfected mystically and wisely according to God. This gathering and union, beyond reason and mind, into the hidden oneness of the divine simplicity, will take place in the

incorruptible age of intelligible realities. In that age, gazing on the light of the invisible and more than ineffable glory, they themselves also become receptive, together with the powers above, of the blessed purity. After this, as the end of all, comes the distribution of the mystery. It transforms into itself those who partake worthily and makes them like the Good that is the cause, by grace and participation, lacking nothing of it as far as is attainable and possible for human beings. So they too can be, and be called, gods by adoption according to grace, because the whole God has wholly filled them and has left no part of them empty of his presence. CHAPTER 22. …of our true God and High Priest. The soul enters, and through the divine readings, which act as symbols, it is taught the principles of beings and the wonderful and great mystery of divine providence revealed in the Law and the Prophets. After each reading it receives from God the peace-giving signs, a reward for its good discipleship in these things. They come through the holy powers, which converse with it spiritually in the mind. With them comes the strengthening and preserving charm of a divine and fiery longing for God, through the delight of the divine songs that are sung to it mystically and spiritually. Then the soul passes on from these things and is gathered up to the one and only summit that holds all these principles together in unity. I mean the holy Gospel, in which all the principles of providence and of beings already exist in unified form, in one power that embraces them. After this, those who love God may again see, by divine perception and with the fearless eyes of the mind, the Word and God himself coming to the soul from heaven. This is what the high priest's descent from the priestly throne signifies. The Word perfectly separates from the soul, as if they were catechumens, the thoughts that still picture sense perception and the division that belongs to it. From there, once the soul has come outside sensible things, as the closing of the doors of God's holy church gives us to understand, he leads it to the knowledge of intelligible things. This knowledge is immaterial, simple, unchanging and godlike, free of every form and shape, and the entrance of the ineffable mysteries reveals it. In this knowledge the soul gathers its own powers into itself and brings itself to the Word. Through the spiritual kiss it unites the ineffable principles and modes of salvation that concern it, and the Word teaches it to confess them with thanksgiving through the symbol of faith. After this, as the soul has now grasped the principles of both sensible and intelligible things in a simple and undivided power, through discipleship and knowledge, he leads it to the knowledge of the theology that has been made manifest. Once it has passed beyond all things, he grants it an understanding equal to that of the angels, as far as it can attain this. And he teaches it, with sobriety, as much as this: to know one God, one essence, three hypostases. He is a monad of essence in three hypostases and a Trinity of hypostases of one essence; a monad in a Trinity and a Trinity in a monad. They are not one and another, nor one beside another, nor one through another, nor one in another, nor one from another. The Godhead is the same in itself, by itself and toward itself, identical with itself, both monad and Trinity. Its union is without confusion, and its distinction is undivided and without parts. It is a monad according to the principle of essence, that is,

the principle of being, but not by composition, contraction or any kind of confusion. It is a Trinity according to the principle of how it exists and subsists, but not by division, estrangement or any kind of partition. For the monad is not divided among the hypostases. It is not present in them by mere relation, or merely observed in them. Nor are the hypostases compounded into a monad, nor do they make it up by contraction. It is the same, identical with itself, though in one way and in another. The holy Trinity of hypostases is a monad, without confusion, in essence and in the simple principle of essence. And the holy Monad is a Trinity in its hypostases and in its mode of existence. The same whole is conceived as this and as that in different ways, according to one principle and another, as has been said. It is one and only Godhead, undivided and unconfused, simple, undiminished and unchanging. As a whole it is a monad in essence, and the same as a whole is a Trinity in hypostases. It is one ray of one thrice-radiant light, shining forth in a single form. After this the soul has received, in equal honor with the holy angels, the principles about the Godhead that are revealed and attainable by creation. It has learned to hymn unceasingly, in harmony with them, the one Godhead in a Trinitarian way. Then it is led to adoption by grace, through a likeness that resembles God. Through this adoption, after the prayers, it has God as Father mystically and by grace alone, and it will be gathered, in ecstasy from all things, into the oneness of his hiddenness. It will undergo divine things rather than know them, so far that it no longer wishes to belong to itself. It cannot be known from itself, by itself or by anyone else, but only by the whole God. He has taken it up wholly, as befits his goodness. He has entered it wholly, as befits God and without passion [variant: has wholly entered it, as befits God], and has deified it wholly. So the soul becomes, as the all-holy Dionysius the Areopagite says, "an image and manifestation of the invisible light, a pure mirror, most transparent, unflawed, undefiled, spotless, receiving the whole beauty of the archetypal good, if one may say so, and shining forth in itself, in a godlike and unchanging way and as far as possible, the goodness of the silence in the inner sanctuaries." CHAPTER 24. [?] … [?] of the rites celebrated according to the worth [?]; among the faithful and those who gather faithfully, the abiding [grace] of the Holy Spirit [?] … The blessed elder therefore thought it necessary, and never stopped urging every Christian, to frequent God's holy Church and never to stay away from the holy synaxis celebrated in it. One reason was the holy angels who remain there and on every occasion record

those who enter, present them to God and make supplications for them. Another was the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is always invisibly present but is present in a special way above all at the time of the holy synaxis. This grace transforms and reshapes each person found there, and truly refashions him toward what is more divine, in proportion to his capacity. It leads him to what the mysteries being celebrated reveal, even if he does not perceive it himself, because he is still one of the infants in Christ and cannot see into the depth of what is happening. It works in him the salvation signified by each of the divine symbols celebrated, advancing in sequence and order from the first things to the end of all. At the first entrance it works the casting off of unbelief and the increase of faith, the lessening of vice and the growth of virtue, the disappearance of ignorance and the addition of knowledge. Through the hearing of the divine oracles it works firm and unchangeable habits and dispositions in the things just named, that is, in faith, virtue and knowledge. Through the divine songs that follow, it works the soul's willing assent to the virtues, and the spiritual pleasure and delight that arise in it [?]. Through the sacred reading of the holy Gospel, it works the end of the earthly mindset, as of a sensible world. Through the closing of the doors that follows, it works the soul's passage and removal, in its disposition, from this corruptible world to the intelligible world. In this passage the soul shuts its senses like doors and makes them pure of the idols of sin. Through the entrance of the holy mysteries, it works a more perfect, more mystical and new teaching and knowledge about God's dispensation toward us. Through the divine kiss, it works an identity of concord, like-mindedness and love: of all with all, of each first with himself, and with God. Through the confession of the symbol of faith, it works fitting thanksgiving for the wondrous ways of our salvation. Through the Trisagion, it works union and equal honor with the holy angels, and the unceasing, harmonious vigor of the sanctifying glorification of God. Through the prayer in which we are counted worthy to call God Father… [Note 58: "truly": A and B read "to speak truly."]

MYSTAGOGY. …the firm and inviolable promise of… [?], which we believe we shall attain if we have kept the commandments as far as we are able. We shall pass from the grace that is in faith to the grace that is in sight. Our God and Savior Jesus Christ will clearly transform us into himself. He will remove from us the marks of corruption and will grant us the archetypes that were shown to us through the sensible symbols here.

To make it easy to remember, if you agree, let us run briefly over the meaning of what has been said and sum it up as follows. The holy Church, as has been said, is a type and image of God. As Creator, by his infinite power and wisdom, he works an unconfused union among the different essences of beings, holding them together around himself at the highest level. In the same way the Church unites the faithful with one another in a single form, through the one grace and calling of the faith. She unites the practical and virtuous through one identity of will, and the contemplative and knowing, in addition, through an unbreakable and undivided concord. She is also a type of the world, both intelligible and sensible: she has the sanctuary as a symbol of the intelligible world and the nave as a symbol of the sensible. Again, she is an image of man, imitating the soul through the sanctuary and presenting the body through the nave. And she is a type and image of the soul itself, considered by itself. Through the sanctuary she bears the glory of its contemplative part, and through the nave the good order of its practical part. As for the holy synaxis celebrated in her: the first entrance signifies, in general, the first coming of our God. In particular, it signifies the conversion of those who, through him and with him, are brought from unbelief to faith, from vice to virtue, and from ignorance to knowledge. The readings that follow it indicate, in general, the divine wishes and purposes by which everyone must be instructed and must live. In particular, they indicate the teaching and progress in faith of those who have believed. For the practical, they indicate the firm disposition of virtue, by which they walk in line with the divine law of the commandments, stand manfully and unshakably against the devil's schemes, and escape the operations that oppose them. For the knowing, they indicate the habit of contemplation, by which the spiritual principles of sensible things and of the providence over them

[?] principles, as far as possible, and are carried unerringly toward the truth. The divine melodies of the songs signify the divine pleasure and delight that arise in the souls of all. Mystically strengthened by this delight, they forget the past labors of virtue and renew their vigorous longing for the divine and pure goods still to come. The holy Gospel, in general, is a symbol of the consummation of this age. In particular, for believers it signifies the complete disappearance of the old error. For the practical, it signifies the mortification and end of the fleshly law and mindset. For the knowing, it signifies the gathering of the many and various principles and their referral to the most comprehensive Principle, once their more discursive and varied natural contemplation has been completed and brought to its end. The high priest's descent from the throne and the dismissal of the catechumens signify, in general, the second coming from heaven of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. They signify the separation of sinners from the saints, and the just repayment of each according to their worth. In particular, for believers they signify the perfect assurance in faith that God the Word brings when he comes invisibly. Through it, every thought that still limps in faith in any way is driven out of them like a catechumen. For the practical, they signify perfect dispassion, through which every passionate and unenlightened thought leaves the soul. For the knowing, they signify the comprehensive knowledge of what has been known, through which all images of material things are chased out of the soul. The closing of the doors, the entrance of the holy mysteries, the divine kiss and the recitation of the symbol of faith signify, in general, several things. They signify the passing away of sensible things and the revelation of intelligible things. They signify the new teaching of the divine mystery that concerns us, and the identity of concord, like-mindedness and love that will come about of all toward all, toward themselves and toward God. They also signify thanksgiving for the ways in which we were saved. In particular, for the faithful they signify progress from simple faith to teaching and initiation in doctrines, to agreement and to piety. The closing of the doors signifies the first of these, the entrance of the holy things the second, the kiss the third, and the recitation of the symbol the fourth. For the practical, they signify the move from practice to contemplation of those who have shut their senses and come outside the flesh and the world by casting off the

activities that belong to the senses. They signify the ascent from the way the commandments are kept to the principle behind them. They signify the kinship and union of the commandments themselves, through their own principles, with the powers of the soul, and the habit suited to theological thanksgiving. For the knowing, they signify the move from natural contemplation to the simple understanding of intelligible things. In this understanding a person no longer pursues the divine and ineffable Word through sense or through anything that appears. They also signify the union of the soul's powers with the soul, and the simplicity that grasps the principle of providence in the mind, in a single form. The unceasing, sanctifying doxology of the holy angels in the Trisagion signifies, in general, the life to come. In the age to come the heavenly and earthly powers will at once and together share an equal way of life, conduct and harmony in the divine doxology. Human bodies will have been made immortal through the resurrection. They will no longer weigh the soul down with corruption, nor be weighed down. Through the change into incorruption they will have received the power and fitness to receive the presence of God. In particular, for the faithful it signifies rivalry with the angels in theology according to faith. For the practical, it signifies an angel-like brilliance of life, as far as this is possible for human beings, and vigor in theological hymnody. For the knowing, it signifies angel-like conceptions, hymns and perpetual movement concerning the Godhead, as far as is possible for human beings. Then come the blessed invocation of the great God and Father, the acclamation "One is holy" and what follows it, and the partaking of the holy and life-giving mysteries. These signify the adoption, union, intimacy, divine likeness and deification that, through the goodness of our God, will come to be over all and in all who are worthy. Through these, God himself will be all in all alike to those who are saved. As the archetypal beauty, he will shine forth as cause in those who, through virtue and knowledge, by grace likewise shine with him. He called the beginners, those making progress and the perfect "faithful," "virtuous" and "knowing." In other words, they are slaves, hired workers and sons, the three orders of the saved. The slaves, the faithful, are those who carry out their master's commandments for fear of the punishments he has threatened, and who work loyally on what has been entrusted to them. The hired workers are those who, out of desire for the promised goods, patiently bear the burden of the day and the scorching heat. This means the affliction that is innate in the present life and yoked to it since the condemnation of our first parents, and the temptations that come with it, for the sake of

virtue. By their own free choice they wisely exchange one life for another, the present life for the life to come. The sons are those who are never separated from God, neither for fear of what is threatened nor for desire of what is promised. They stay with him through the disposition and habit of the soul's willing inclination toward the good. They are like the son to whom it was said, "Child, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours." By grace and adoption, as far as possible, they are what God is, and is believed to be, by nature and as cause. Let us not, then, stay away from God's holy Church. In the holy order of the divine symbols celebrated in her, she contains so many mysteries of our salvation. Through them she fashions each of us in Christ in proportion to himself, especially the one who lives well. And she brings to light the gift of adoption, given through holy baptism in the Holy Spirit, in the one who lives in Christ. Instead, with all our strength and zeal, let us show ourselves worthy of the divine gifts and please God by good works. Let us not behave like the Gentiles, who do not know God, in the passion of lust. As the holy Apostle says, we must put to death "the members that are on earth: fornication, impurity, passion, evil desire and covetousness, which is idolatry, on account of which the wrath comes upon the sons of disobedience," and also "all anger, rage, filthy talk" and lying. In short, let us put off "the whole old man, which is corrupted by deceitful desires, with his deeds" and desires, and "walk worthily of God, who called us into his kingdom and glory." Let us put on "heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, meekness and patience, bearing with one another in love, and forgiving each other if anyone has a complaint against another, just as the Lord also forgave us." Above all, let us put on "the bond of perfection," love, and the peace "to which we were also called in one body." To sum it up, let us put on "the new man, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image [?] of the one who created him." If we live this way, we may be able to reach the goal of the divine promises with good hope, and "be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, bearing fruit and growing in the knowledge of the Lord, strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory, for all edification and patience with joy, giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit for a share in the inheritance of the saints in the light." A clear proof of this grace is a willing fellow-feeling, through goodwill, toward those who share our nature. Its work is to make our own, as God does and as far as we can, any person who needs our help in any way. We must not leave him neglected and uncared for, but must show with fitting zeal, in action, that our disposition toward God and our neighbor is alive in us. For action is the proof of a disposition. Nothing makes righteousness so easy, and nothing is so well suited to deification (if I may put it that way) and to nearness to God, as mercy offered from the soul to those in need, with pleasure and joy. The Word showed that the one who needs to be treated well is God, for he says, "Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me." And the one who said this is God. Much more, then, will he show that the one who is able to do good, and does it, is truly God by grace and participation. Such a person has taken on, in imitation [?], God's own activity and property of doing good. The poor man is God because of the condescension of God, who became poor for our sake. He takes on himself, in sympathy, the sufferings of each person, and until the end of the age he always suffers mystically, out of goodness, in proportion to the suffering in each one. If, then, the poor man is God, it is all the more reasonable that the one who is a god is the one who, imitating God out of love for humanity, heals the sufferings of those who suffer through himself, in a godlike way. Such a person shows that, in his disposition, he has the same power as God, by analogy with God's saving providence. Who, then, is so slow and sluggish toward virtue that he does not desire divinity, when it is so cheap, so easy to obtain and so easy to acquire? There is a safe and inviolable guard for these things, and an easy road to salvation. Without it, I think, none of the good things a person has will truly be kept unharmed. It is minding one's own business, or attending to one's own affairs. Through it we learn to look at and examine only our own affairs, and so we are freed from suffering pointless harm from others. If we learn to see and examine only ourselves, we shall never attack the affairs of others, however they may stand [?]. We know that there is only one wise and just judge, God. He judges wisely and justly everything that happens according to the principle by which it came about, not according to the way it appeared. Human beings might perhaps be able to judge the way it appeared, looking dimly at the outward appearance. But the truth by no means always lies there, nor does the principle behind what happens. God sees the hidden movement of the soul, its unseen impulse, the very principle by which the soul was moved, and the aim of that principle, that is, the end conceived beforehand for every action. He judges… [Notes: ⁸⁵ "clearly then" (δὲ δηλονότι): A. ⁸⁸ "preconceived" (genitive form): C. A.] PATROLOGIA GRAECA 91.

[?]justly, as I said, all the things that human beings do. If we strive to achieve this, we will also keep ourselves within ourselves and not cling to outward things. We will not let the eye, the ear or the tongue see, hear or speak of the affairs of others. If possible, we will not let them do so at all. If not, we will let them act in such matters with compassion rather than passion, and we will allow them to see, hear and speak only for our own profit, and only as far as seems good to the divine Word who holds their reins. For none of these organs slips more easily into sin when reason does not train it, and again none is readier for salvation when the Word orders and regulates them and leads them where they must go and where he wills. So let us not neglect, as far as we are able, to obey God, who calls us to eternal life and a blessed end through the practice of his divine and saving commandments, so that we may receive mercy and find grace to help us in time of need. For grace, says the divine Apostle, is with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. That is, it is with those who love the Lord with the incorruption that comes from virtue and with a pure and unfeigned holiness of life, by doing his will and not corrupting any of his divine commands. I have set out these things on these matters for the sake of the reward of obedience, as well as I could and as I was taught. I have not dared to touch the more mystical and lofty matters. If any lover of learning longs to know them, let him read what holy Dionysius the Areopagite wrote on these matters with divinely inspired labour. There he will find a true revelation of ineffable mysteries, granted to the human race through his divine mind and tongue for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation. If this has not fallen far short of your desire, thanks be to Christ, the giver of good things, and to you who reminded me to speak of these things. But if it falls somewhere far short of what you hoped, what am I to suffer, or what am I to do, since I am weak in speech? For weakness deserves pardon, not punishment, and what is possible and within one's reach deserves acceptance rather than blame. This is especially true for you, who have resolved to love for God's sake. And to God everything offered genuinely from the soul, according to one's power, is dear, even if it seems small when compared with great things. He did not reject even the widow who brought the two mites. Whoever this widow was, and whatever the two mites were, she may be a soul widowed of wickedness. Such a soul has cast off the old law as though it were a husband, but it is not yet worthy of full union with the Word and God. Even so, it offers to him, by way of [a pledge?]

…as it were mites, the following things. These may be the reason and life it has had so far in due measure, or faith and a good conscience. They may be the settled habit of good things and the practice of them, or the contemplation and action suited to these, or the corresponding knowledge and virtue. Or they may be the things a little beyond these, by which I mean the principles in the natural and the written law. Having acquired these, the soul offers them, because it wishes to be united to the Word and God alone by going out of them in ecstasy and letting them go, as if they were its whole life and existence. It accepts being widowed of the constraining ways, statutes and customs of nature and the law, as though they were husbands. Or the two mites may be something else, more spiritual than these, at which the word hints only to those who are pure in mind, through the letter fulfilled [in history?]. For when all the things that seem great in virtue among human beings are compared with the contemplative word of theology, they turn out to be small. Yet even though they are small and made of cheap material of little value, they still bear the royal stamp just as much as the gold coins of more precious matter that the wealthier offer. And perhaps they carry more, namely the intention of the woman who offers them out of her whole disposition. Imitating this widow, I too have offered to God and to you, beloved, these small and cheap thoughts and words like mites, concerning the things you commanded. They have come forth from a cheap and poor mind and tongue. I beg your blessed and holy soul two things. First, do not seek any further written record of anything I say, and this for two reasons. The first reason is that I have not yet acquired the pure fear of God that endures forever. Nor have I gained a firm habit of virtue or a stable and unshaken grounding in true righteousness, and these are the things that most of all bear witness to the reliability of words. The second reason is that I am still tossed about by a great surge of passions, like a wild sea. I am far from the divine harbour of dispassion, and the end of my life is uncertain. So I do not wish to have my words in writing as an accuser, in addition to my deeds. Second, accept these things for the sake of my obedience, if that is fitting, and commend me in your prayers to Christ, the great and only God and Saviour of our souls. To him be glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, unto the ages. Amen.
